description:
We’re a group of university students interested in technology, space, data, and creative problem-solving. We’re excited to take on a real-world challenge, learn from each other, and build something meaningful together.

Our team has interests and experience in areas like AI, data science, and software.
summary: Microgravity Fire Safety is an interactive dashboard that presents NASA’s scattered knowledge on microgravity combustion in a clear Fire-Safety answer for human space flights. It extracts information from 40 different experiments conducted from ISS to Shuttle era only using the values from NASA experiments. The fire simulator is its central feature. Users select the environment (space, Moon, Mars, or Earth) and a type of material that has already been tested in the experiments. The simulator investigates the behaviour of that fire, and a superintelligent agent sends an alarm to the monitoring station on Earth taking into account the time delay, and the agent takes action independently (without human intervention) in order to put the fire out. The Simulation Risk Tracker is the tool keeping track of the pressure, oxygen concentration, partial pressure, airflow, and all other factors, which contribute to a score, showing how dangerous an area is concerning fire. The SI agent is honest about data gaps in the NASA database, for instance: there are no experiments conducted on fire in partial gravity for the Moon or Mars, so it is classified as extrapolated and every experiment has a confidence score in relation to these environments. This is important as astronauts will soon be inhabiting these environments where fire behaviour has not been studied and astronauts far from earth cannot await instructions in case of a fire emergency.
details:
What does it do?

The Microgravity Fire Safety Dashboard offers a compilation of NASA fire-related research with 40 experiments ranked from 1 to 10, based on their impact on fire danger on Moon and Mars spacecrafts and habitats. It allows users to browse through the information by type and material and features an easy-to-read summary with a reference to the NASA source, graphs, and an assistant tab.

The main part of the system is the Simulation Risk Tracker. The user starts with choosing one of four environments: space, Moon, Mars or Earth (gravity varying from 0-1g). The tracker receives cabin pressure, oxygen level, oxygen partial pressure, ventilation and airflow, and material flammability level measurement and distance from the heat source in centimetres. It calculates the fire hazard score reflecting the probability of fire occurrence in specific conditions, simulates how it would develop and uses a self-operating SI agent to suppress the fire.

What benefits does it have?

This involves transforming dispersed research into an indexed, searchable list that can be utilized in mere minutes by the students, researchers, and engineers. The risk tracker facilitates users in testing the "what if" scenarios like increased oxygen levels or decreased airflow conditions, and then they can see the modifications of the hazards accordingly. Each row is linked to the source from NASA.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Astronauts stationed on the Moon and Mars will deal with fires under unfamiliar and unstudied conditions. The project shows ways the conditions can increase fire risk, as well as how the system might react independently with a record of every action.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The dashboard is a web application that can run on any browser, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used Claude, an artificial intelligence assistant from Anthropic, when writing code for the app and when designing its layout, including a list with rankings, filters, charts, risk simulator and alarm logs. When creating plain-language experiment summaries and 1 to 10 safety scores from each experiment’s abstract, we employed Google Gemini API, followed by a manual revision from our science lead. The dashboard is hosted on GitHub with the help of GitHub pages available for free public access. The data used in every experiment comes from NASA databases and reports, including the Physical Science Informatics database (PSI), NASA Technical Reports Server and NASA Science pages, and every experiment links back to its source. No additional hardware equipment was required.

How is your project creative?

Most research dashboards stop at displaying data. Our system goes beyond that; it utilizes NASA’s experiments as a tool for people to work with. The same factors used by NASA in its experiments (the oxygen concentration, the pressure, the direction of flow of the air, the combustion material, as well as its distance from the source of heat) are controlling variables in the Simulation Risk Tracker that we have developed. It allows users to simulate different environment conditions (e.g. space, Moon, Mars or Earth) and see the change in the fire hazard score. Furthermore, we took into account that there is a particular delay of transmission of information from Mars (it usually takes about 3 to 22 minutes), so we designed an autonomous SI agent, which is able to detect the fire, send alerts and act, and all decisions can be analysed and replayed through logs. The scoring system is applied to the Moon and Mars as well in this project; every experiment (40 experiments in total) is scored according to its impact on fire safety in lunar and Martian conditions.

What factors did your team consider?

- Targeted audience: The text was created for teachers, pupils, researchers and engineers, so we’ve simplified the language and employed convenient filters to make finding the necessary information easy.

- Verification process: Every experiment directly refers to the exact NASA publication, so users can carry out their own verification.

- Data gaps: The problem is that no partial-gravity combustion information is available from NASA for Moon and Mars yet, and our data is just an approximation.

- Score limitations: The hazard score helps compare conditions, but it can’t be regarded as a precise prediction of the fire occurrence.

- Safety measure: This project is an educational application, and it can’t be considered a fire safety measure.

- Potential for improvements: We can integrate new experiments as soon as NASA gets the partial-gravity combustion information without the need to change the dashboard structure.
